# Pulmonary edema

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Other pulmonologic disorders > Pulmonary edema*

[Original Article Link](/library/Us0b8h)

---

## Summary

Pulmonary <u>edema</u> is the accumulation of fluid in the <u>lung</u> <u>interstitium</u> and <u>alveoli</u>. Causes can be broadly classified as cardiogenic, most commonly <u>acute decompensated heart failure</u> (e.g., due to <u>acute myocardial infarction</u>), and noncardiogenic, most commonly <u>ARDS</u> (e.g., due to <u>pneumonia</u>). Clinical features include progressive <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>signs of hypoxemia</u> (e.g., <u>cyanosis</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>), and features of the underlying cause, such as <u>S3 gallop</u> on <u>cardiac auscultation</u> in <u>cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u>. <u>Laboratory studies</u> (e.g., <u>BNP</u>, <u>cardiac biomarkers</u>) and imaging studies (e.g., <u>chest x-ray</u>, <u>POCUS</u>) are performed to help determine the underlying cause and confirm the diagnosis. Management often involves hemodynamic and <u>respiratory support</u> to prevent and treat <u>respiratory failure</u>. The decision of whether to use pharmacotherapy and which agent to use depends on the cause.

---

## Etiology

The etiology of pulmonary <u>edema</u> is multifactorial in ∼ 10% of patients. [[2]](/library/DJc1wW0)




| <br>Cardiogenic vs. noncardiogenic pulmonary edema [[2]](/library/DJc1wW0)[[3]](/library/9JcNwW0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Cardiogenic pulmonary edema | Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema |
| Description | <br>* An accumulation of low-protein fluid in the <u>interstitium</u> and <u>alveoli</u> due to an increase in pulmonary <u>capillary</u> <u>hydrostatic pressure</u><br><br> | <br>* An accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the <u>lung</u> <u>interstitium</u> and <u>alveoli</u> due to an increase in permeability of the pulmonary <u>capillaries</u><br><br> |
| Pathophysiology | <br>* Imbalance of hydrostatic and <u>oncotic pressure</u> between the pulmonary <u>capillaries</u> and <u>interstitial space</u> → disturbed net filtration of fluid → accumulation of extravascular fluid<br><br> |  |
| Etiology | <br><br>* <u>Causes of acute heart failure</u> (<u>left ventricular</u> systolic and/or <u>diastolic dysfunction</u>), e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Acute coronary syndrome</u><br><br>* Acute <u>myocarditis</u><br><br>* Nonischemic <u>cardiomyopathy</u><br><br>* Circulatory overload, e.g.:<br><br>* IV <u>fluid overload</u><br><br>* <u>TACO</u><br><br>* <u>Cardiorenal syndrome</u> (type 3 or type 4)<br><br>* <u>Valvular dysfunction</u>, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Aortic regurgitation</u> or stenosis<br><br>* <u>Mitral regurgitation</u> or stenosis<br><br>* <u>Cardiac arrhythmia</u>, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Atrial fibrillation</u> with a rapid ventricular response<br><br>* <u>Ventricular tachycardia</u><br><br>* <u>Third-degree AV block</u><br><br>* <u>Hypertensive emergency</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pneumonia</u><br><br>* <u>Inhalational injury</u><br><br>* <u>Reexpansion pulmonary edema</u><br><br>* <u>ARDS</u><br><br>* <u>Sepsis</u><br><br>* <u>Acute pancreatitis</u><br><br>* <u>Shock</u><br><br>* <u>Preeclampsia</u><br><br>* <u>Blood transfusion</u>-related <u>acute lung injury</u> (<u>TRALI</u>)<br><br>* Neurological injury (<u>neurogenic pulmonary edema</u>)<br><br>* <u>Upper airway</u> obstruction<br><br>* <u>High-altitude pulmonary edema</u> (<u>HAPE</u>)<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Pulmonary and nonpulmonary causes of <u>noncardiogenic pulmonary edema</u> can occur simultaneously.

---

## Clinical features

* General symptoms [[2]](/library/DJc1wW0)

* Progressive <u>dyspnea</u> and/or <u>tachypnea</u>

* <u>Cough</u>, possibly with pink frothy <u>sputum</u> or expectoration

* <u>Fever</u> (e.g., secondary to <u>pneumonia</u> or <u>sepsis</u>)

* <u>Physical examination</u> findings [[2]](/library/DJc1wW0)[[4]](/library/wJchwW0)

* <u>Signs of hypoxia</u> (e.g., <u>cyanosis</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>)

* <u>Agitation</u>, <u>diaphoresis</u> and/or confusion

* Dullness upon <u>chest wall</u> percussion

* Increased <u>tactile fremitus</u>

* Inspirational <u>crackles</u> on <u>lung auscultation</u>

* In <u>cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u>:

* <u>S3 gallop</u> or <u>murmurs</u> on <u>cardiac auscultation</u>

* <u>Jugular vein distention</u>

* <u>Peripheral edema</u>

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles




* The diagnosis of pulmonary <u>edema</u> is usually confirmed by imaging, e.g., <u>chest x-ray</u>, <u>lung POCUS</u>.

* Additional studies (e.g., <u>BNP</u>, <u>ECG</u>) can help identify the underlying cause.

* There is no single test to distinguish <u>cardiogenic vs. noncardiogenic pulmonary edema</u>.





### Imaging studies




#### <u>Chest x-ray</u> [[2]](/library/DJc1wW0)[[3]](/library/9JcNwW0)[[5]](/library/stWtUM0)




* Indication: all patients with suspected pulmonary <u>edema</u>

* Views: PA, <u>lateral</u>, or AP

* Typical findings in cardiogenic pulmonary edema 

* Opacities in the perihilar areas (bat wing pattern)

* Kerley B lines: horizontal, linear opacities that represent thickened interlobular septa; 1–2 cm in length and perpendicular to the pleural surface

* <u>Pleural effusions</u>

* Enlarged <u>cardiac silhouette</u>

* <u>Peribronchial cuffing</u>

* Findings suggestive of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema 

* Peripheral, patchy <u>ground-glass opacities</u>

* Peripheral <u>air bronchograms</u> and <u>pulmonary consolidations</u>

#### Other studies




* Indications: as an alternative to <u>chest x-ray</u> or to further assess radiographic abnormalities

* Modalities

* <u>Lung POCUS</u>: <u>B lines</u> and <u>pleural effusions</u>  [[5]](/library/stWtUM0)

* CT chest: similar findings to plain film, with higher resolution

### Additional assessment




### Routine studies [[6]](/library/aKWQUm0)[[7]](/library/bmWHVN0)




Results from the following studies can help to rule out common causes of pulmonary <u>edema</u>:




* <u>ECG</u>: <u>ECG findings in STEMI</u>, <u>ECG findings in AHF</u> [[5]](/library/stWtUM0)

* <u>Cardiac biomarkers</u>

* <u>BNP</u> ;  [[6]](/library/aKWQUm0)[[7]](/library/bmWHVN0)

* < 100 pg/mL: suggestive of <u>noncardiogenic pulmonary edema</u>

* > 400 pg/mL: suggestive of <u>cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u>

* ↑ <u>Troponin T/I</u>, <u>CK-MB</u>, and/or <u>myoglobin</u>: suggestive of <u>cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u>  [[2]](/library/DJc1wW0)

* <u>Blood gas analysis</u>: <u>Respiratory failure</u> and/or <u>acid-base disorders</u> may be present.

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>Leukocytosis</u> may be present in many causes of pulmonary <u>edema</u>, e.g., <u>sepsis</u>, <u>acute pancreatitis</u>, and <u>ACS</u>.

* <u>BMP</u>

* ↑ <u>Creatinine</u> in <u>kidney</u> disease

* <u>Serum osmolality</u> and/or <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities in IV fluid overload





### Additional studies [[2]](/library/DJc1wW0)




Consider the following based on clinical suspicion:




* <u>Lipase</u>, <u>amylase</u>: to rule out <u>acute pancreatitis</u>

* <u>Blood cultures</u> and <u>gram stain</u>: to assess for <u>bacteremia</u> and <u>sepsis</u>

* <u>Echocardiography</u>: to assess for <u>left ventricular</u> <u>systolic dysfunction</u> and/or <u>valvular dysfunction</u>

* CT <u>brain</u>: if <u>neurogenic pulmonary edema</u> is suspected

* <u>Pulmonary artery catheterization</u> (<u>gold standard</u>) if findings from other studies are inconclusive and results of catheterization would affect management  [[2]](/library/DJc1wW0)[[5]](/library/stWtUM0)

---

## Management

### Approach




* Provide <u>respiratory support</u> as needed.

* <u>Supplemental oxygen</u>

* Ventilatory support (invasive or noninvasive)

* See “<u>Respiratory support in AHF</u>” and “<u>Lung-protective ventilation strategies</u>” for more information.

* Treat the underlying cause (e.g., <u>AHF</u>, <u>ARDS</u>, <u>HAPE</u>).

* Maintain adequate <u>perfusion</u> (e.g., with <u>IV fluids</u>) to prevent <u>end-organ damage</u> in patients with <u>noncardiogenic pulmonary edema</u>.

* Tailor pharmacotherapy based on the complete clinical picture.





> [!WARNING]
> For patients with respiratory and/or <u>hemodynamic instability</u>, involve a critical care specialist early (e.g., <u>rapid response team</u>).




### Pharmacotherapy




Indications for pharmacotherapy vary based on the underlying disease process. See disease-specific articles for dosing.




* <u>Loop diuretics</u> (e.g., <u>furosemide</u>)

* First line for <u>cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u>

* May be considered for other causes of pulmonary <u>edema</u> (e.g., <u>ARDS</u>) if there are <u>signs of fluid overload</u>

* See also “<u>Pharmacotherapy for HF</u>” and “<u>Diuretics for AHF</u>.”

* <u>Vasodilators</u> (e.g. IV <u>nitroglycerin</u>)

* First-line for <u>cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u> caused by a <u>hypertensive emergency</u>

* Decreases <u>preload</u> and <u>pulmonary congestion</u>

* See also “<u>Vasodilators for AHF</u>.”

* <u>Inotropes</u> (e.g., <u>dobutamine</u> or <u>dopamine</u>) for patients with low systolic blood pressure

* <u>Nifedipine</u> OR <u>phosphodiesterase inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>sildenafil</u>) for <u>HAPE</u> if immediate descent and <u>oxygen therapy</u> are not feasible

* <u>Opioids</u> (e.g., <u>morphine</u>) may be used for <u>palliative treatment of dyspnea</u>  [[7]](/library/bmWHVN0)[[8]](/library/SpYyKJ)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Diuretics</u> and vasoactive drugs can cause <u>hemodynamic instability</u> and are not appropriate for all causes of pulmonary <u>edema</u> (e.g., <u>HAPE</u>, <u>reexpansion pulmonary edema</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Opioids</u> have historically been used to treat acute pulmonary <u>edema</u>.

## Flash pulmonary edema

* Description

* Sudden-onset, potentially life-threatening <u>cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u> that can cause acute <u>hypoxemic respiratory failure</u>

* Can occur in <u>de novo heart failure</u> and <u>acute decompensated heart failure</u> (<u>ADHF</u>)

* <u>Risk factors</u> [[11]](/library/xycEhU0)

* Long-standing poorly controlled <u>hypertension</u> [[10]](/library/kibm7t)

* <u>LVH</u> and <u>diastolic dysfunction</u>

* Bilateral <u>renal artery stenosis</u> [[12]](/library/oAc0kU0)

* <u>Coronary artery disease</u>

* <u>Obstructive sleep apnea</u>

* Triggers: similar to those of <u>ADHF</u> [[11]](/library/xycEhU0)

* <u>Sympathetic</u> activation: exertion, <u>sympathomimetics</u> (e.g., <u>cocaine</u>), medication nonadherence, psychosocial <u>stress</u> or <u>anxiety</u> [[10]](/library/kibm7t)

* Abrupt hemodynamic changes

* <u>Hypertensive emergency</u>

* <u>Volume overload</u>

* <u>Myocardial</u> <u>ischemia</u>

* Acute <u>mitral regurgitation</u>

* <u>Tachyarrhythmias</u>

* Pathophysiology: Multiple processes lead to a vicious cycle of sympathetically-driven ↑ <u>LVEDP</u> and pulmonary <u>edema</u>. [[10]](/library/kibm7t)[[11]](/library/xycEhU0)

* Long-term <u>hypertension</u> → ↑ <u>atherosclerosis</u> and <u>cardiac remodeling</u> → ↑ <u>afterload</u> and ↑ <u>MVO<sub>2</sub></u>, <u>LVH</u>, and ↑ <u>diastolic dysfunction</u>

* <u>Sympathetic</u> activation → peripheral and <u>splanchnic</u> vasoconstriction→ ↑ <u>venous return</u> and ↑ <u>afterload</u> → ↑ pulmonary <u>edema</u> and ↓ <u>cardiac output</u>

* ↑ Pulmonary <u>edema</u> and ↓ <u>cardiac output</u> → <u>end-organ dysfunction</u> and <u>hypoxemia</u> → ↑ <u>sympathetic</u> activation

* Clinical features [[8]](/library/SpYyKJ)

* <u>Hypertension</u>, <u>hypoxia</u>

* Features of <u>pulmonary congestion</u>: e.g., <u>crackles</u>, <u>signs of increased work of breathing</u>, <u>respiratory distress signs</u>

* Minimal <u>peripheral edema</u>

* See also “Wet and warm” in “<u>Classification of acute heart failure</u>.”

* Diagnostics: similar to other types of pulmonary <u>edema</u>

* <u>CXR</u>: <u>x-ray</u> findings in <u>pulmonary congestion</u>

* <u>Ultrasound</u> 

* <u>B lines</u> often present on <u>lung</u> <u>ultrasound</u> (See “<u>POCUS in acute heart failure</u>” for details)

* <u>Echocardiography</u>: See “<u>Echocardiographic findings in AHF</u>.”

* Management: See “<u>Management of acute heart failure</u>.”

* Stabilization with <u>NIPPV</u> and <u>vasodilators for ADHF</u>  [[8]](/library/SpYyKJ)[[11]](/library/xycEhU0)

* Treatment of the underlying condition and trigger management.
